### Contributing guidelines

- [X] I have read [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

### Module(s)

mini.animate

### Question

I've wanted to try `mini.animate` module but found a weird behavior when doing centered jumps.

I've fixed my `<C-f>` bind according to `mini.animate` docs:

```vim
<cmd>lua vim.cmd('normal! <C-f>'); MiniAnimate.execute_after('scroll', 'normal! zz')<cr>"
```

The problem is that I still have a weird animation behavior when jumping from a start of a document to center:


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d90a7c9e-de9e-4d11-9a25-a75b068fcf4e

comment_data.body:
Yeah, I can reproduce. The reason this seems to happen is that centering afterwards itself triggers an animation.

To be perfectly honest, scrolling animation from 'mini.animate' is far from perfect if you want to follow it with `zz`. The suggested solution somewhat works with `n` and `N`, but might have troubles with `<C-f>` / `<C-d>` / etc.

My suggestion would be to either not do the centering or disable scroll animation entirely (however painful it is for me to say this).

comment_data.body:
I’ve run into this issue before in the past. This discussion prompted me to take another look to see if there was a workable workaround.

My approach so far is to replace the default scroll keymaps with linewise equivalents that mimic the default behavior.

See:
`:h scroll-down`
`:h scroll-up`

1 . Put the module below somewhere in your config (e.g. `utils/window-scroll.lua`).
2.  Use the exposed functions directly to create keymaps, or make a `map_scroll_keys` method to map them.

```lua
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Window scroll module
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

local M = {}
local H = {}

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Page movement
-- Help tags:
--  :h scroll-up
--  :h scroll-down
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Move the cursor vertically by a given number of lines.
---@param count integer Number of lines to move
---@param direction '"down"'|'"up"'
H.move_lines = function(count, direction)
  -- stylua: ignore
  if count <= 0 then return end

  local motion = direction == "down" and "j" or "k"
  vim.cmd("normal! " .. count .. motion)
end

--- Calculate the number of lines for a page-sized movement.
---@param size '"full"'|'"half"' Page size to calculate
---@return integer lines
H.get_page_size = function(size)
  local height = vim.api.nvim_win_get_height(0)

  if size == "half" then
    return math.floor(height / 2)
  end

  return height - 2
end

--- Move the cursor down by one full page.
M.page_down = function()
  H.move_lines(H.get_page_size("full"), "down")
end

--- Move the cursor up by one full page.
M.page_up = function()
  H.move_lines(H.get_page_size("full"), "up")
end

--- Move the cursor down by half a page.
M.half_page_down = function()
  H.move_lines(H.get_page_size("half"), "down")
end

--- Move the cursor up by half a page.
M.half_page_up = function()
  H.move_lines(H.get_page_size("half"), "up")
end

return M
```
### Example `map_scroll_keys` method
```lua
--- Overwrite all default scroll keymaps
M.map_scroll_keys = function()
  local page_down_lhs = { "<S-Down>", "<kPageDown>", "<PageDown>", "<C-f>", "<S-CR>", "<S-+>" }
  for _, lhs in ipairs(page_down_lhs) do
    vim.keymap.set({ "n", "v" }, lhs, M.page_down, { desc = "Scroll page down" })
  end
  vim.keymap.set({ "n", "v" }, "<C-d>", M.half_page_down, { desc = "Scroll half page down" })

  local page_up_lhs = { "<S-Up>", "<kPageUp>", "<PageUp>", "<C-b>", "<S-->" }
  for _, lhs in ipairs(page_up_lhs) do
    vim.keymap.set({ "n", "v" }, lhs, M.page_up, { desc = "Scroll page up" })
  end
  vim.keymap.set({ "n", "v" }, "<C-u>", M.half_page_up, { desc = "Scroll half page up" })
end
```

### Example `keymaps.lua`
```lua
local scroll = require("utils.window-scroll")

-- stylua: ignore start
vim.keymap.set({ "n", "v" }, "<PageDown>", scroll.page_down, { desc = "Scroll page down" })
vim.keymap.set({ "n", "v" }, "<C-f>", scroll.page_down, { desc = "Scroll page down" })
vim.keymap.set({ "n", "v" }, "<C-d>", scroll.half_page_down, { desc = "Scroll half page down" })

vim.keymap.set({ "n", "v" }, "<PageUp>", scroll.page_up, { desc = "Scroll page up" })
vim.keymap.set({ "n", "v" }, "<C-b>", scroll.page_up, { desc = "Scroll page up" })
vim.keymap.set({ "n", "v" }, "<C-u>", scroll.half_page_up, { desc = "Scroll half page up" })
-- stylua: ignore end
```

reply_data.body: If this approach works here, that's great. However, moving cursor up/down is not the same as scrolling the page. For example, if cursor is at the top of the window, then moving it half window lines down won't scroll the window at all. There would have to be some aggressive centering done before and after, right?

reply_data.body:
Hey @echasnovski , sorry for the delayed response.

> However, moving cursor up/down is not the same as scrolling the page. For example, if cursor is at the top of the window, then moving it half window lines down won't scroll the window at all.

You're right. I misunderstood the help documentation (embarrassingly enough on the first sentence 😅 ).

From `:h scrolling`:

```help
These commands move the contents of the window.  If the cursor position is
moved off of the window, the cursor is moved onto the window (with
'scrolloff' screen lines around it)
```

As you explained before: moving the cursor is not the same as scrolling. Cursor movement only causes a scroll once the cursor goes off-screen.

To better understand why `zz` after a scroll behaves the way it does, I set the scroll `duration` to a high value (1000ms). Seeing it visually cleared it up for me:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6ae80dfb-c339-4499-8f77-81f4dff336ad

As showcased in the video: scroll commands move the window contents in one direction, while `zz` re-centers the cursor by moving the window contents in the opposite direction. When both are ran in quick succession, it causes the undesired bounce effect.

A workaround I've started to experiment with is to temporarily disable `mini.animate` for the `zz` step using a deferred callback.

I don't know the exact math/timing, but with the default 250ms `duration`, 9 ms seems to be the breakpoint where disabling/re-enabling prevents the second `zz` scroll.

```lua
local cb = function()
  vim.b.minianimate_disable = true
  vim.cmd("normal! zvzz")
  vim.defer_fn(function()
    vim.b.minianimate_disable = false
  end, 10)
end

-- example setting keymaps with mini.animate's `execute_after` method
vim.keymap.set("n", "<C-f>", function()
  vim.api.nvim_feedkeys(vim.api.nvim_replace_termcodes("<C-f>", true, false, true), "n", false)
  MiniAnimate.execute_after("scroll", cb)
end, { desc = "Scroll full page down" })

-- or run the call back in an autocmd (my preference)
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("User", {
  group = vim.api.nvim_create_augroup("mini_animate", { clear = true }),
  pattern = "MiniAnimateDoneScroll",
  desc = "Center after scroll",
  callback = cb,
})
```
Edit: This was working reasonably well when I sent a message via `vim.notify` after the deferred callback. My guess is the notification forces a redraw or schedule that affects the timing. Back to the drawing board for now
